annotations.keyFindings: Direct-to-CT on the ambulance stretcher and pre-notification cut the median door-to-needle time from 58 to 36 minutes; within-45-minute treatment rose from 31 to 69 percent; treated mimics rose from 2 to 5 percent.
annotations.limitations: Single-centre before-and-after report; other changes may have contributed.

annotations.keyFindings: Across 160 timed cases, arrival-to-CT (median 17 minutes) and CT-to-decision (median 14 minutes) were the largest delays; late drug preparation added 7 minutes; a single group page shortened arrival-to-CT.
In 3,420 cases, out-of-hours door-to-needle time was 12 minutes longer, most where the registrar was on call from home.
annotations.limitations: Cannot separate staffing from imaging availability.

annotations.keyFindings: Across 22 improvement reports, symptomatic haemorrhage did not rise in any, while treated mimics rose in four, up to 6 percent.
annotations.limitations: Reports underpowered for haemorrhage; selective reporting likely.

annotations.keyFindings: Case-by-case run charts detect a sustained 15-minute improvement within about 20 cases; monthly medians need five to six months.
annotations.limitations: Simulation and 30-hospital data; assumes stable case mix.

annotations.keyFindings: Two-minute nurse-led debriefs followed 81 percent of cases and were seen as blame-free; needle times fell 9 minutes alongside other changes.
annotations.limitations: Two hospitals; effect of debriefs not separable.

claims.text: At a regional stroke centre, direct transfer to CT on the ambulance stretcher and pre-notification reduced median door-to-needle time from 58 to 36 minutes over 18 months.

claims.interpretation: Direct-to-CT is the first change to test.

claims.passage: The largest delays occurred between arrival and CT (median 17 minutes) and between CT and the treatment decision (median 14 minutes).
claims.interpretation: Map these two intervals in detail first.

claims.text: In a regional dataset of 3,420 thrombolysis cases, median door-to-needle time was 12 minutes longer at night and at weekends.
claims.passage: median door-to-needle time was 12 minutes longer at night and at weekends than in weekday daytime
claims.interpretation: Plot out-of-hours cases distinctly on the run chart.

claims.text: Across 22 improvement reports, symptomatic haemorrhage did not rise in any report, while treated stroke mimics rose in four, reaching 6 percent in one.
claims.passage: Symptomatic haemorrhage did not rise in any report, while treated mimics rose in four reports, reaching 6 percent in one.
claims.interpretation: Track both as balancing measures with numerators and denominators.

claims.text: Case-by-case run charts of door-to-needle times detect a sustained 15-minute improvement within about 20 cases, whereas monthly medians need five to six months.

synthesis: Six retrieved records, appraised at abstract level; four model leads remain unverified and are not appraised. Direct-to-CT transfer with pre-notification cut median door-to-needle time from 58 to 36 minutes at a comparable regional centre, and time studies place most delay between arrival and CT and between CT and the decision, with late drug preparation and serial paging adding minutes. Out-of-hours cases are 12 minutes slower where the registrar is on call from home. Treated mimics can rise with faster pathways, so they and haemorrhage are balancing measures. Case-by-case run charts suit a centre treating seven or eight patients a month.
gradeRationale: Improvement reports and observational time studies, mostly single-centre and uncontrolled; consistent direction for pathway changes, low certainty about effect size here.
summary: Six retrieved records appraised; five claims; overall certainty low; leads left unverified.
